issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not reverse a trial court’s factual finding based on oral evidence and witness credibility when the finding rests on proper appreciation of the evidence and no sufficient reason displaces it.
material_facts: The trial court considered the material on record and found that the claimant had possessed the property until she was dispossessed.
The trial court’s finding relied in part on its assessment of the credibility of witnesses.
The appellate court reversed that finding without due regard to the probabilities of the case and the considerations that had weighed with the trial court.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court should not have reversed the trial court’s finding of possession, and its judgment could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles governing appeals on fact, including Sections 96–100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court may review evidence but should ordinarily give due weight to the trial judge’s advantage in observing witnesses. Under Sarju Pershad v. Raja Jawaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh, a finding turning on credibility should not be reversed unless a special feature escaped the trial judge or a sufficient balance of improbability displaces the trial judge’s assessment.

rule.if: appeal_from_trial_finding and oral_credibility_material and trial_court_properly_assessed_evidence and no_sufficient_reason_to_displace_finding

predicates.appeal_from_trial_finding: A party appealed a trial court’s factual finding.
predicates.oral_credibility_material: The finding depended materially on oral testimony and the credibility of witnesses.
predicates.trial_court_properly_assessed_evidence: The trial court considered the material evidence and assessed the witnesses before reaching its finding.
predicates.no_sufficient_reason_to_displace_finding: No special feature or sufficiently strong improbability justified displacing the trial court’s assessment.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a properly assessed trial finding that materially depends on witness credibility, and no sufficient reason displaces that finding, the appellate court should not reverse it.

issues.legal_issue: A title holder retains constructive possession of vacant land that is rendered incapable of use by submersion unless another person has already acquired title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The claimant established title to a vacant, low-lying property that was seasonally submerged and incapable of ordinary use and enjoyment.
The land was described as a pit or pond and was otherwise vacant.
The opposing parties did not establish that they had acquired title by adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: Possession continued constructively with the title holder; the seasonal submersion did not itself interrupt that possession or establish adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Possession continues with the title holder unless and until another person acquires title by adverse possession. Where land is submerged and incapable of use or enjoyment, constructive possession remains with the title holder, provided the title was not extinguished by adverse possession before the last submersion. Seasonal submersion is not different in principle from prolonged submersion. The Court relied on Basanta Kumar Roy v. Secretary of State, including its discussion of Leigh v. Jack and Secretary of State for India v. Krishnamoni Gupta, and on the general rule stated in Sarkar on Evidence that possession of part may constitute possession of the whole where the whole is otherwise vacant.

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit and claimant_proved_title and property_otherwise_vacant and land_submerged_and_unusable and not defendant_acquired_adverse_title

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession of land.
predicates.claimant_proved_title: The claimant established title to the land.
predicates.property_otherwise_vacant: The property was otherwise vacant rather than occupied or used by another person.
predicates.land_submerged_and_unusable: The land was submerged in a way that made it incapable of use or enjoyment.
predicates.defendant_acquired_adverse_title: The opposing party acquired title to the land by adverse possession before the relevant submersion.

issues.definition: In a possession-recovery proceeding, a claimant who proves title retains constructive possession of otherwise vacant land made unusable by submersion unless the opposing party has already acquired title by adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: A case should not be remanded to allow a party to make good an evidentiary failure on adverse possession when that party was not misled and had an opportunity to present its evidence.
material_facts: The trial court did not frame an issue on whether the opposing parties had perfected title by adverse possession.
The opposing parties produced no evidence supporting their plea of adverse possession.
They did not claim that they had been misled in presenting their case or denied an opportunity to adduce evidence.
On appeal, they sought a remand to establish adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused to remand the case to allow the opposing parties to make good their evidentiary lapse.
issues.legal_principle: A remand is not warranted merely to give a party another opportunity to repair a failure to produce evidence where the party was neither misled nor denied the opportunity to present its case.

rule.if: appeal_with_remand_request and adverse_possession_pleaded and no_evidence_supporting_plea and party_not_misled and party_had_opportunity_to_present_evidence

predicates.appeal_with_remand_request: An appeal includes a request to remand the case for further proceedings.
predicates.adverse_possession_pleaded: A party asserted that it acquired title by adverse possession.
predicates.no_evidence_supporting_plea: The party produced no evidence to support its adverse-possession plea.
predicates.party_not_misled: The party was not misled in how it presented its case.
predicates.party_had_opportunity_to_present_evidenc: The party had an opportunity to present evidence on its plea.

issues.definition: When a party seeks a remand to support an adverse-possession plea despite having presented no supporting evidence, the case should not be remanded if the party was not misled and had an opportunity to present that evidence.
